{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-az-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"aaf6bd823e048982e03427c5b42bec5b8641c26f5fc55141f83c0297fecf97a2","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-az-class-d:lineage:69","source_registry_sha256":"6dbbc2d22fea619728bdb90038a4aedf3afc07eab652b3f97027c9c69aaadaf4","source_liveness_sha256":"1c5753487760cbe2044d84b5696121c7181af61815b598d89d5ce158abf5fe43"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Braking and stopping distance, following distance, rural driving, weather, sun glare, wind, dust storms, rain and hydroplaning","heading":"C — What controls stopping distance, perception and reaction time, following distances, open-road hazards, driving in bad weather, sun glare, wind and trailers, Arizona dust storms, rain and hydroplaning","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — What controls stopping distance, perception and reaction time, following distances, open-road hazards, driving in bad weather, sun glare, wind and trailers, Arizona dust storms, rain and hydroplaning
Knowledge domain: the factors that set how far a car travels before it stops, average perception and reaction times, how much following distance to keep and when to add more, hazards on empty rural roads, how weather, glare and wind change your driving, what to do in an Arizona dust storm, and how to drive in rain without hydroplaning.

FACT_ID: sec16-F01 | anchor: A01
Bringing a vehicle to a safe, complete stop takes a long distance. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F02 | anchor: A01
Braking distance depends on your speed, your perception and reaction times, the pavement, your tires, your vehicle's weight including any load or trailer, and the type and condition of your brakes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F03 | anchor: A01
Perception time, the time it takes a driver to see and recognize a dangerous situation, averages 0.75 seconds. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F04 | anchor: A01
Reaction time, the gap between perceiving danger and starting to brake, averages 0.75 seconds. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F05 | anchor: A01
On average a person needs 1.5 seconds to perceive a threat in the roadway and react to it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F06 | anchor: A01
Knowing how far your vehicle needs to stop helps you pick a safe driving speed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F07 | anchor: A01
The manual's stopping-distance chart is only a guide, because your real stopping distance depends on factors such as your tires, brakes and the road. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F08 | anchor: A01
Keep a following distance of at least 3 seconds in most driving situations, so you can avoid a crash if traffic ahead stops suddenly. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F09 | anchor: A01
Some situations call for a longer following distance of 3 to 6 seconds. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F10 | anchor: A01
On slippery roads, double your following distance to 6 seconds or more so you have room to adjust your speed or stop. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F11 | anchor: A01
If the driver behind you wants to pass, slowing down lets that driver get by sooner and gives more room to pull back into the lane. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec16-F12 | anchor: A02
When a large vehicle such as a tractor-trailer blocks your view ahead, drop back farther so you can see around it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F13 | anchor: A02
A quiet, empty rural highway can carry as much danger as busy city traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F14 | anchor: A02
Common rural hazards include animals on the road, slow farm equipment just past the top of a hill, and low spots covered with water. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F15 | anchor: A02
On open rural roads, stay alert, watch for warning signs and slow down as you near curves or hills that hide the road ahead. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F16 | anchor: A02
In bad weather, poor visibility and poor traction often happen at the same time. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F17 | anchor: A02
Changing road and weather conditions shorten the time you have to react and affect how your car handles. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F18 | anchor: A02
In bad conditions the first rule is to reduce speed, which offsets the visibility and reaction time you have lost. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F19 | anchor: A02
Driving toward the sun in the early morning or late afternoon creates glare. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F20 | anchor: A02
Sunglasses, clean windows and sun visors all help cut down sun glare. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F21 | anchor: A02
When the sun is behind you, oncoming drivers may be facing the glare and may not see your car or your signals. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F22 | anchor: A02
Strong winds, and crosswinds in particular, make a vehicle harder to control. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F23 | anchor: A02
Wind is very dangerous for campers, large recreational vehicles and anyone towing a trailer, and it also makes lightweight vehicles harder to control. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F24 | anchor: A02
To gain more control in a strong wind, slow down. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F25 | anchor: A02
When you leave a sheltered stretch for open space, expect crosswinds that may push you toward the side or the middle of the road. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F26 | anchor: A02
Wind may make a vehicle that is pulling a trailer sway. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec16-F27 | anchor: A03
Gusts created by large trucks or buses you meet may force you to make steering corrections. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F28 | anchor: A03
Wind currents can cause a vehicle pulling a trailer to jackknife. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F29 | anchor: A03
If you are towing a trailer and a truck or bus passes on your left, move as far right in your lane as you can and slow down, then speed up gently as it goes by so the trailer tracks straight. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F30 | anchor: A03
Driving into a strong headwind may take more acceleration and makes steering harder. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F31 | anchor: A03
A tailwind pushes your speed up, so you must slow down and start braking earlier to stop. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F32 | anchor: A03
Dust storms are common in Arizona and can sometimes cut a driver's visibility to zero. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F33 | anchor: A03
If you run into a dust storm, check the traffic around you at once and begin slowing down. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F34 | anchor: A03
Pull off the road as soon as you can in a dust storm, rather than waiting until poor visibility makes it hard to do safely. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F35 | anchor: A03
In a severe dust storm, slow down immediately, drive all the way off the highway and stop as far to the right as you can. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F36 | anchor: A03
During a dust storm, never stop in a travel lane or in the emergency lane. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F37 | anchor: A03
After pulling off in a severe dust storm, turn your lights off and take your foot off the brake. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F38 | anchor: A03
Stay inside the vehicle with seat belts buckled until the dust storm has passed. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F39 | anchor: A03
Heavy rain is especially hazardous when it comes with gusty winds, as in a thunderstorm. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F40 | anchor: A03
In heavy rain, vehicles behind you and in your blind spots are especially hard to see. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F41 | anchor: A03
Wait a short time after rain begins before switching on your wipers, because blades on a dirty windshield can smear it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F42 | anchor: A03
In rain, slow down so the gap to the vehicle ahead grows to at least 6 seconds. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F43 | anchor: A03
Take extra care in the first 30 minutes of rain, when road grime and oil mix with water and make the surface slippery. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F44 | anchor: A03
In heavy rain, tires can ride up on a film of water, and at 50 mph they can lose all contact with the road. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F45 | anchor: A03
Tires that are under-inflated, worn or bald lose contact with a wet road at much lower speeds. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec16-F46 | anchor: A03
Slowing down is the best way to prevent hydroplaning. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

Misconceptions: in a dust storm you do not keep your lights on once you are parked off the road, you turn them off and take your foot off the brake; the stopping-distance chart is a guide, not a promise; the first minutes of rain are the most slippery, not the safest; a tailwind lengthens your stop rather than shortening it.
Mnemonics: Pull Aside, Stay Alive for dust storms; see it, react, then brake; tailwind means brake early, headwind means more gas and harder steering.
Glossary: perception time means the time to notice and recognize a danger; reaction time means the time from noticing a danger to starting to brake; hydroplaning means tires riding on a film of water and losing grip; jackknife means a trailer swinging sideways against the towing vehicle; crosswind means wind blowing across your path.
Dynamic facts: dust storm guidance and following-distance advice can be revised by the issuer, and the average stopping figures come from federal tests that may be updated.
